title: Observation and control of polariton noise in a thermal Rydberg atom electrometer
authors: Teng Zhang, Luís Felipe Gonçalves, Alisher Duspayev, Georg Raithel, David A. Anderson
abstract: The establishment of metrics and control of fundamental noise sources in quantum sensing is a long-standing goal in quantum science and technology. We report on the observation of polariton-mediated optical noise in a thermal Rydberg atom vapor and demonstrate its active control and suppression using a radio-frequency field in Rydberg electrometry. The noise exhibits structured amplification and reduction across the Rydberg electromagnetically induced transparency resonance. This reveals a nonlinear slow-light feedback mechanism in which the polariton medium stores and releases probe-field energy. We show that the reference radio-frequency field used in Rydberg heterodyne receivers can also tune the medium into an operating regime where high electromagnetic-field responsivity coincides with reduced optical noise. This operating-point control enables optimization of the electric-field sensitivity within the constraints imposed by Rydberg-polariton physics. These results establish polariton noise as a previously unrecognized intrinsic noise source in thermal Rydberg vapors and the corresponding control method as a crucial aspect of continued efforts to achieve fundamental sensitivity limits in Rydberg electrometry.
summary: This paper reports the observation and active control of polariton-mediated optical noise in a thermal Rydberg atom electrometer. By exploiting the nonlinear slow-light feedback mechanism inherent to the EIT resonance, the authors demonstrate how applying a reference RF field can suppress this noise. This establishes polariton noise as a critical, controllable factor for improving the sensitivity of Rydberg-based quantum sensors.
main_problem: The primary goal is to establish metrics and actively control fundamental noise sources, specifically polariton-mediated optical noise, within quantum sensing platforms.
main_result: The authors successfully observed and demonstrated active suppression of this intrinsic polariton noise by applying a resonant radio-frequency field, optimizing the electric-field sensitivity of the Rydberg electrometer.
method: The study combines experimental measurements of noise spectra with theoretical modeling using a phenomenological slow-light feedback picture derived from the density matrix formalism.
model_or_system: The system utilizes a thermal Rydberg atom vapor undergoing Electromagnetically Induced Transparency (EIT), which supports the formation and propagation of polaritons. The dynamics are modeled using the density matrix formalism and Lindblad equation.
key_observables: Polariton noise (AC component), EIT absorption dip (DC component), group velocity ($v_g$), and the ratio of noise suppression/amplification across the EIT resonance.
important_parameters: Coupler detuning ($\Delta_c$), Rabi frequencies ($\Omega_p, \Omega_c$), and the operating regime defined by the feedback mechanism ($v_g > 0$ and $dv_g/d\Omega_p < 0$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a phenomenological slow-light feedback picture rather than a complete quantum model, and the noise dips are noted to be surprisingly narrow.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the measured EIT absorption and polariton noise spectra versus detuning, alongside calculated plots of absorption, refractive index, and group velocity, mapping the noise suppression regions to the negative feedback regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the noise problem in the Rydberg electrometer, presenting experimental measurements of noise structure across the EIT resonance, developing a theoretical model linking noise to slow-light feedback, and concluding with the demonstration of active noise control.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles fundamental noise limitations in quantum sensing using controlled light-matter interactions in Rydberg media, providing a concrete mechanism (negative feedback) to approach fundamental sensitivity limits.
